There are a few major shortcomings that must be addressed before publication which include the
fact that:
(i) there is a lack of power calculations, and it is often not clear how many technical replicates were
done. Is the study not under-powered? If it is this should be clearly stated and conclusions;
Response: We acknowledge that a priori power calculations were not performed for the initial
animal studies. In direct response to this comment, we have significantly enhanced the statistical
foundation of our study through the following substantive expansions:
• We supplemented the original 100 whole blood samples with an additional 192 clinical serum
samples, providing enhanced statistical power for the quantitative comparison between our
method and the clinical gold standard (immunoturbidimetry).
• The mouse cohort for the LPS-induced inflammation model (Fig. 2) was increased from n=4 to
n=12 per group, providing robust statistical power for the comparisons made in this model.
• The animal numbers in the 4T1 tumor model (Fig. 3) were increased from n=1 to n=3 per group.
We understand that this sample size remains limited for rigorous inter-group comparisons,
reflecting the practical challenges associated with these long-term, high-cost longitudinal
experiments. We have explicitly clarified in the Revised Manuscript that the primary aim of this
particular experiment was to demonstrate the unique capability of our platform for long-term
dynamic monitoring with minimal sample volumes, and we have exercised caution in drawing
conclusions based on this small sample size. This point is now discussed as a study limitation.
Regarding technical replicates: We apologize for the previous lack of clarity. We have now explicitly
stated throughout the Methods section and figure legends that while each biological sample was
typically assayed once on the array, each analyte was measured in quadruplicate spots within that
single assay. The final data point for each sample represents the mean fluorescence intensity
calculated from these replicates after applying a robust outlier exclusion method (removing the
spot with the highest deviation). This approach ensures measurement reliability while conserving
precious biological samples.
These enhancements to statistical power and methodological clarity have been fully detailed in our
responses to related revisions.
(ii) the use of a ROC analysis is actually inappropriate and should be removed – these “curves” are
based on a single point;
Response: We fully concur with the reviewer's expert assessment that presenting a single optimal
cut-off point as an ROC "curve" was statistically inappropriate. In accordance with this
recommendation, we have removed the ROC curve from Fig. 4 and implemented the following
revisions:
• We now report the diagnostic sensitivity and specificity values, along with their corresponding
95% confidence intervals (calculated using the Clopper-Pearson exact method), directly in both the
main text and the Fig. 4 legend.
• We explicitly state that the optimal cut-off value was determined by maximizing Youden's index
(J) from the dataset.
• Throughout the Revised Manuscript, we have eliminated any reference to an "ROC curve" and
instead describe the process objectively as "determining the optimal diagnostic cut-off through
Youden's index analysis."
These modifications ensure proper statistical reporting while maintaining the validity of our
diagnostic performance assessment.
As noted in our other responses, these statistical corrections have been comprehensively
addressed throughout the revised manuscript.
(iiii) from a robust statistical viewpoint, the data could be re-presented using a Bland Altman
analysis, with confidence intervals and error bars shown on all figures throughout
Response: We thank the reviewer for these excellent suggestions to enhance the robustness of
our data presentation. We have implemented these changes as follows:
• Bland-Altman analysis: We have now performed Bland-Altman analysis for all key method-
comparison experiments. For the comparison between the DBDIY array and immunoturbidimetry
for CRP detection (192 serum samples), a Bland-Altman plot is now included as Fig. 4h.
These plots display the mean bias and the 95% limits of agreement (±1.96 SD), providing a clear

sample size for the experiment presented in Fig. 2. The study now includes 12 mice per group
(control and LPS-injected), up from the initial 4, and this is clearly stated in the revised figure legend.

excluded, and the mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) was calculated from the remaining three
spots, as described in the Methods. This approach provides a reliable technical measurement for
each biological replicate while conserving precious sample volume. The increased sample size
(n=12 biologically independent samples per group) now provides substantial power for the
statistical comparisons made.

Response: We thank the reviewer for raising these important methodological considerations
regarding the comparison with CBA. We acknowledge the observed quantitative differences
between the platforms, where the absolute concentrations measured by our DBDIY array were
generally lower than those obtained by CBA (Fig. R2). This discrepancy can be reasonably attributed
to several methodological factors.
First, there are inherent standardization differences between the platforms, as each employs
distinct antibody pairs and reference standards calibrated through independent systems.
Second, the fundamental detection principles differ substantially. CBA utilizes bead-based
fluorescence detection in solution, whereas our DBDIY platform relies on surface-based capture
combined with plasmon-enhanced fluorescence, which may affect binding kinetics and signal
generation. Finally, matrix interactions and solid-phase binding efficiency may vary between the
two systems, potentially influencing absolute recovery rates.
Despite these expected technical variations in absolute quantification, it is important to emphasize
that both platforms demonstrated excellent concordance in detecting the same biological trends.
All seven cytokines showed statistically significant and consistent elevation patterns in response to
anti-CD3/28 stimulation across both methods.
While a formal matrix effects study was beyond the scope of this initial technology validation, the
consistent response patterns observed across multiple cytokines in complex cell culture
supernatants provide indirect evidence that matrix effects are comparably managed in both
systems.
The consistent biological conclusions drawn from both platforms, despite technical differences in
absolute quantification, strongly support the validity and utility of our DBDIY array for functional
immune monitoring applications where relative changes and response patterns are of primary
importance.

In direct response to this concern, we have provided three supplementary videos that visually
demonstrate the operational workflow. Supplementary Video 1 illustrates the complete DBDIY
process, showing how a standard pipette interacts with our patterned chip. Supplementary Video
2 specifically highlights the system's built-in tolerance to pipetting position deviations, confirming
that the hydrophilic-hydrophobic interface effectively self-guides and confines droplets even with
intentional misalignment. Most notably, Supplementary Video 3 demonstrates continuous manual
spotting of over 100 spots in a routine and efficient manner, providing direct evidence of the
method's practicality.
These visual demonstrations are supported by quantitative data in Supplementary Fig. 1, where
we deliberately introduced positional deviations and found no significant impact on final
fluorescence signals. This confirms that the chip's patterned design provides intrinsic spatial
guidance, making the process robust to normal variations in manual pipetting.

results. This stands in clear contrast to systems requiring expensive, high-precision robotic

Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding protein stability during drying, which is indeed a critical consideration for any solid-phase immunoassay. In response to the question of whether drying such surfaces without protective layers is normal practice, we would like to clarify that the process of drying spotted capture antibodies to immobilize them on a solid surface is in fact a well established and widely used method in the fabrication of both commercial and research based protein microarrays (Ref. 17-29).
In our current protocol, the capture antibodies were prepared in a standard phosphate buffered
saline (PBS) solution. The chemical composition of the spotting buffer, including ionic strength and
pH, plays a key role in helping maintain protein structural integrity during the brief drying and
immobilization process. This conventional approach has proven effective for laboratory based
immunoassays, as supported by the high sensitivity and specificity achieved in our study. These
performance metrics confirm that under our controlled conditions, the drying process did not
compromise the assay's functionality.
Looking ahead, we completely agree that developing a formulation for robust, long-term storage
is a vital next step. This would vitrify upon drying, creating a protective microenvironment around
the immobilized antibodies and enabling the development of a ready-to-use, shelf-stable product.

Reviewer #3:
Thank you for the authors’ efforts in revising the manuscript. The additional data and clarifications
have improved several aspects of the work and in general, the paper is an example of good
scientific work. However, some important points related to the clinical relevance, interpretation of
diagnostic performance, and methodological transparency remain insufficiently addressed.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the constructive feedback and for acknowledging the
improvements made. We agree that clinical relevance, diagnostic performance interpretation, and
methodological transparency are essential for evaluating any novel diagnostic platform. Below we
address these points in detail.
• Clinical relevance and diagnostic performance interpretation
We recognize that direct comparison of absolute concentration values between different
immunoassay platforms can be challenging due to inherent variations in reagents, detection
principles, calibration, and data processing. Therefore, in validating our DBDIY platform, we
focused on demonstrating its ability to accurately reflect clinically relevant biological trends rather
than pursuing perfect numerical agreement with a reference method that uses fundamentally
different reagents and detection principles.
This approach is well established in the validation of novel diagnostic technologies, as it prioritizes
correct identification of biomarker patterns, such as elevated CRP during infection or cytokine
dynamics upon immune stimulation, over absolute concentration concordance. Our results show
strong correlation (R² > 0.9) and acceptable limits of agreement in Bland-Altman analysis across a
large cohort of clinical samples, confirming that the DBDIY platform reliably captures the same
biological variations as the clinical reference method. This supports its suitability for clinical
screening and longitudinal monitoring in volume-limited settings.
• Enhancing methodological transparency
To further improve transparency, we have now clearly specified both concentration-based and raw-
signal-based cutoff values. We have also converted the fluorescence signals for CRP and NT-proBNP
into concentration units to facilitate visual assessment of diagnostic agreement. Statistically
inappropriate ROC curve depictions have been removed and replaced with confidence intervals
and Bland-Altman analyses. These revisions provide a clearer and more statistically rigorous
presentation of the platform’s diagnostic performance and enhance the reproducibility of our
assay protocol.
We believe these clarifications and additions have strengthened the clinical relevance and
methodological transparency of our study, and we thank the reviewer for prompting these
important improvements.
- Abstract: the concept of high-throughput measurement of protein levels in small-volume
biological fluids does not seem compatible with the expression “especially in children (neonates?),
specific disease patients, and experimental animals.” In the context of clinical diagnosis and
laboratory testing, it is not clear how experimental animals are relevant. This may be of greater
importance in the field of intensive care (ICU).
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful observation regarding the phrasing in the
Abstract. The original wording did indeed conflate two distinct application contexts, which could
lead to ambiguity. To clarify the scope and relevance of our platform, we have revised the sentence
to clearly separate its clinical diagnostic value (particularly for vulnerable populations including
children and critically ill patients) from its preclinical utility (enabling longitudinal monitoring in
experimental animals). This modification ensures that the distinct importance of small-volume,
high-throughput protein measurement in each setting is unambiguously communicated.

Response: We thank the reviewer for raising the point regarding the different cutoff lines in Fig. 4b.
The visual distinction arises because the two lines are plotted using different units. The DBDIY
cutoff is drawn based on the corresponding raw fluorescence signal, while the clinical cutoff is
reported as a concentration. This presentation choice was intentional, as we sought to avoid
potential bias introduced by inter-platform variations in standard sources, detection principles,
calibration models, and data processing, all of which can complicate direct concentration-based
comparisons.
To validate the quantitative performance of the DBDIY platform, we collected 112 pediatric
peripheral blood samples and measured CRP using both the DBDIY array and the clinical dry
fluorescence immunoassay (DFIA). To minimize the influence of differences in reference standards,
we constructed the calibration curve using samples with known clinical values. The derived
concentration results, as shown in Fig. 4, demonstrate that the DBDIY platform achieves 100%
sensitivity and specificity (95% CI: 95.2 to 100%) and a high correlation (R² = 0.940) with the clinical
method, whether based on raw fluorescence signals or on concentration values.
The strong concordance between the raw DBDIY signal and the clinical concentration indicates that
the platform can support semi-quantitative analysis and longitudinal monitoring without requiring
a standard curve (Supplementary Fig. 6). This feature is particularly valuable in resource-limited
settings, where results can be interpreted visually from the fluorescence pattern for relative trend
assessment. In laboratory or clinical settings requiring precise quantification, concentration values
can be obtained reliably via the standard calibration curve and data processing.
In summary, the use of raw signal for cutoff visualization reflects our methodological approach to
cross-platform comparison, while the additional validation with 112 samples confirms the
platform’s robust quantitative performance and operational flexibility.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In their paper, Yue et al. present a “droplet-based do-it-yourself” (DBDIY) protein array platform utilizing a patterned plasmonic substrate. Their approach simplifies and increases sensitivity of the multiplexed immunoassays using low sample volumes. The platform does not rely on traditional spotting and incubation but rather uses confined droplet patterning and plasmonic-enhanced near-infrared fluorescence (NIRF) to enhance signal sensitivity. The authors show some applications, including detection of cytokines in blood, within cell cultures, etc. Finally, the authors report dynamic cytokine profiling and C-reactive protein (CRP) detection from as little as 1 nL of whole blood.

The study is technically solid, with a well-designed experiments and good validation. The manuscript contributes to the field of miniaturized immunoassays and has potential relevance for translational applications, especially in resource-limited diagnostic environments. I therefore can recommend the manuscript for publication, provided the following concerns and inconsistencies have been solved:

1. The authors report 100% sensitivity and specificity, but fail to provide confidence intervals. Furthermore, the reported R² value of 90.3% suggests the presence of discrepancies. Please calculate and include confidence intervals and clarify how statistical robustness was evaluated.
2. It is unclear how the analytical detection limit for CRP was determined. Please describe the methodology used to establish the detection limit, including any calibration curves and statistical thresholds.
3. Blood volume discrepancy in abstract ("with a required serum/blood volume of only 6 µL per test...") vs methods ("60 µL taken at each sampling via retro-orbital bleeding"). Resolve the apparent inconsistency between the stated minimal volume requirement and the actual sampling protocol.
4. The ROC curve was generated after excluding 24 samples. The justification ("clinical method did not provide clear values") is vague. Recommendation: Provide a more detailed explanation of the exclusion criteria and how they may impact the interpretation of diagnostic performance.
5. It is currently unclear whether the fluorescence intensity values reported in Figure 5 can be quantitatively converted into analyte concentrations. The authors should clarify whether fluorescence intensity values can be directly converted to absolute concentrations (e.g., pg/mL). If conversion to pg/mL is possible, present a representative example (e.g., calibration curve used for CRP measurements, including the concentration points, curve fit (e.g., linear, 4-parameter logistic), and associated statistics (R², LOD, LOQ)). If such conversion is not possible with the current data, this should be explicitly stated and discussed as a limitation.
6. Supplementary tables lack units for CRP. The CRP cut-off used in Fig. 4b is not explained.
The authors should clearly define the units and describe how clinical or analytical thresholds were determined. Define the threshold values for presented clinical applications and their basis (e.g., literature, ROC-derived, clinical standard)
7. What equipment was used for pipetting (e.g., Nanoplotter), see Fig 4? Please discuss reproducibility and potential variability across arrays.
8. Include a reference or detailed methodology explaining how the amplification was quantified (the manuscript reports a 240-fold signal amplification using TA-GNP).
9. Blurred Spots in Fig. 1i: Are the spots still evaluable despite blurring? Is there supporting data on reproducibility or signal consistency? Address the reliability of such spots and whether they influence quantitation.
10. The sentence "It was found that DBDIY not only reduced the concentration of CAb but also maintained a total mass of CAb comparable to commercial plotters" is unclear. Clarify whether quantification was performed and specify the values if available.
11. The method and experimental details about the fabrication of the array are not complete and need to described in detail. Silanization process is either not described or wrong (“trifluoro (1H, 1H, 2H, 2H-perfluorooctyl) silane (PFOCTS) (L.98)” should be probably trichloro... silane). The authors should describe in detail how the fabrication procedure was done. Including silanization etc.including silanization, patterning etc.
12. The manuscript mentions "low production costs" and minimal need for specialized personnel. No cost comparison to commercial systems is provided. Pipetting 0.2 µL across ~100 spots requires skills—can this realistically be performed by non-specialists? The authors should provide a cost analysis and discuss the operational feasibility in real clinical laboratory or field settings.
13. Plasmonic-enhanced NIRF is a highly specialized technology, requiring sophisticated equipment. The DIY nature of the array seems at odds with the complexity of the readout system. The authors should either rename the method or explain and discuss the practicality of implementing this platform in low-resource or point-of-care settings.
14. Most clinical laboratories use quantitative high-sensitivity CRP (hsCRP) assays based on immunoturbidimetry, ELISA, or nephelometry, which report concentrations in mg/L or pg/mL. The developed CRP assay is compared against a qualitative reference assay. Without comparing the DBDIY assay to such established quantitative methods, it is difficult to assess its clinical relevance, especially for applications like cardiovascular risk assessment or sepsis monitoring, where precise CRP levels are critical.
Provide justification for this comparison, or if possible, re-analyze the CRP data using a quantitative clinical reference method to provide a more meaningful benchmark. Clearly report the analytical performance parameters of the platform: LOD, LOQ, precision (intra-/inter-assay CV), and linear range. If only a qualitative comparison is possible at this stage, clearly state this limitation and discuss its implications for future validation.
English grammar in some places of the manuscript needs to be improved. For example: “accurate measurement of high-throughput protein levels” (p 2), etc. Please check the grammar throughout the MS.
It should be specified what kind of “contact angle” was used in the characterization (advancing, stating, water, etc.).

### Reviewer 2

The authors should be congratulated on an interesting piece of research, which, I believe after further improvement will be a substantive contribution to the field. The work combines the enhancement of plasmonic arrays with hydrophobic/ hydrophilic interfaces to create an easy-to-use, yet sensitive platform. Both of the initial techniques are well known, however their integration is technically astute in enabling the level of control of surface properties on a plasmonic substrate. This is therefore a clever miniaturisation of a popular technique used in laboratories and serves to minimise reagent consumption.
In general the ideas and results presented are strong in concept, illustrated with a well-conceived assay and underpinned by strong materials engineering.
However, I have a number of general and more specific suggestions.
As a starting point, I think the biological/clinical validation could be stronger (for example, colloidal gold immunochromatography is not a gold standard for CRP and the authors may have chosen an established ELISA). Can they clearly justify their choice?
There are also statistical issues throughout the paper, which are exacerbated by the small sample sizes and in many cases unclear presentation (e.g. in the figure legends).
There are a few major shortcomings that must be addressed before publication which include the fact that:
(i) there is a lack of power calculations, and it is often not clear how many technical replicates were done. Is the study not under-powered? If it is this should be clearly stated and conclusions;
(ii) the use of a ROC analysis is actually inappropriate and should be removed – these “curves” are based on a single point;
(iiii) from a robust statistical viewpoint, the data could be re-presented using a Bland Altman analysis, with confidence intervals and error bars shown on all figures throughout
Some specific comments relevant to each figure/experiment:
Fig 2: It seems like there are 4 mice per group? (authors need clear labels in legend). This is probably under-powered and care needs to be taken when drawing conclusions from this number. How many technical replicates were run.
Fig 3: There are no error bars, no confidence intervals, and definitely no proper statistical testing for the temporal changes. For a 40-day longitudinal study, where is the quantitative analysis of stability or drift over time? Again, this is a small sample size for this type of analysis.
Fig 4: As mentioned, colloidal gold is not a clinical gold standard for CRP, and so a comparison to this alone weakens the claims. There is no explanation for how the positive/negative thresholds were set.
Fig 5: There is missing statistical analysis for method agreement with CBA. No assessment of measurement range differences or matrix effects between platforms was performed.
Below are a few further points that need addressing
Although the authors claim you only need a pipette, it is likely that the spotting inside the arrays is difficult by hand (and indeed in the supplementary they show some holders to do it). Although these are not expensive, but they are not ‘just a pipette’.
It would be useful to comment on drying of the devices for storage and testing. The use of water and the binders could denature the proteins on the surface. Is it normal to dry such surfaces without protective layers?
The patient studies are not described in the Methods and this will be required/important (were the studies blinded?) Ethics is stated in the acknowledgement and does not include inclusion/exclusion criteria.

Response: We thank the reviewer for these important statistical suggestions regarding confidence intervals and the interpretation of the R² value. We have addressed these points as follows:
1. Confidence intervals for sensitivity and specificity
We have now calculated and included the 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for sensitivity and specificity using the Clopper-Pearson method, which is specifically recommended for binomial proportions with our sample size. For both sensitivity and specificity (50/50 correct classifications), the 95% CIs are [92.9%, 100%]. These values have been added to the Results section and the Figure 4 legend to provide a more statistically robust interpretation of our diagnostic accuracy data.
2. Clarification on R² value and statistical robustness
Regarding the R² value of 0.903, we appreciate the opportunity to clarify that this represents strong agreement between methods. The observed discrepancies primarily reflect the enhanced sensitivity of our DBDIY platform in the low concentration range. Specifically, for samples where the reference method approached its detection limit, our array provided more precise quantitative measurements, leading to minor deviations that actually demonstrate our method's superior performance in this critical range. This enhanced low-end sensitivity represents a key advantage rather than a limitation in method agreement.

The analytical detection limit (LOD) for CRP was determined empirically from the calibration curve.
Specifically, a series of CRP standard solutions at known concentrations were analyzed to generate
the calibration curve. The LOD was then calculated as the concentration corresponding to the mean
fluorescence intensity of the blank samples (5% BSA) plus three times its standard deviation. This
value was interpolated from the calibration curve.

Response: We thank the reviewer for these insightful comments regarding the practical
implementation and cost-effectiveness of our DBDIY platform. We have addressed these points in
detail below:
• Cost analysis and comparison to commercial systems
We agree that a quantitative cost analysis is important. The primary cost advantage of our platform
lies in the elimination of two major capital expenditures: the automated nano-plotter (which can
cost $50,000 - $100,000 USD) and the specialized incubation framing systems. In contrast, the core
consumable is our patterned plasmonic chip.
A preliminary cost breakdown for the DBDIY array is as follows:
Patterned Plasmonic Chip: $30-50 per chip (based on raw material and fabrication costs).
Assay Reagents: Comparable to standard immunoassay reagent costs.
Equipment: Requires only a standard electronic pipette (a ubiquitous tool in clinical and research
labs, $500 - $2,000) and a fluorescence scanner.
When compared to a commercial high-throughput protein array system, which requires a
significant initial investment in the plotter and reader (often exceeding $150,000), our platform
offers a reduction in initial capital outlay of over 90%.
• Operational feasibility and skill requirements
Concerning operational feasibility, we acknowledge that manual pipetting of 0.2 µL could present
challenges. However, we have introduced low-cost, reusable positioning guides, demonstrated in
Supplementary Video 1, to facilitate rapid and accurate alignment without requiring specialized
skills. More importantly, the hydrophilic-hydrophobic patterned surface itself provides inherent
tolerance to positioning variations. As systematically evaluated in Supplementary Video 2, even
with deliberate pipetting deviations, droplets are effectively guided and confined to intended areas
without affecting assay performance, as further supported by Supplementary Fig. 1.
Furthermore, Supplementary Video 3 demonstrates continuous manual spotting of over 100 spots
smoothly and efficiently, confirming the practicality and robustness of this process for non-
specialists.
In summary, the DBDIY platform significantly lowers both cost and technical barriers, making it
highly suitable for resource-limited settings, satellite clinics, or research laboratories without
access to core facilities.

14. Most clinical laboratories use quantitative high-sensitivity CRP (hsCRP) assays based on
immunoturbidimetry, ELISA, or nephelometry, which report concentrations in mg/L or pg/mL. The
developed CRP assay is compared against a qualitative reference assay. Without comparing the
DBDIY assay to such established quantitative methods, it is difficult to assess its clinical relevance, especially for applications like cardiovascular risk assessment or sepsis monitoring, where precise CRP levels are critical.
Provide justification for this comparison, or if possible, re-analyze the CRP data using a quantitative clinical reference method to provide a more meaningful benchmark. Clearly report the analytical performance parameters of the platform: LOD, LOQ, precision (intra-/inter-assay CV), and linear range. If only a qualitative comparison is possible at this stage, clearly state this limitation and discuss its implications for future validation.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this critical suggestion regarding the need for
comparison with established quantitative methods. We fully agree that such validation is essential
for assessing the clinical relevance of our CRP assay, particularly for applications requiring high
sensitivity such as cardiovascular risk assessment. In direct response to this comment, we have
conducted an additional comprehensive validation study comparing our DBDIY array against
immunoturbidimetry, the standard quantitative method for high-sensitivity CRP (hs-CRP) testing in
clinical laboratories.
This comparison was performed using 192 clinical serum samples specifically intended for hsCRP
analysis. The results demonstrate excellent quantitative agreement between the two methods:
• The correlation coefficient reached 0.973 (Fig. 4g)
• Bland-Altman analysis revealed a minimal mean bias of -0.96%, with the vast majority of data
points falling within the ±1.96 SD limits of agreement (Fig. 4h)
Furthermore, we have now explicitly reported the complete analytical performance parameters of
our platform for CRP detection:
• Limit of Detection (LOD): 9.573 pg mL⁻¹
• Limit of Quantification (LOQ): 20.273 pg mL⁻¹
• Linear Range: The working range spans from the LOD up to 64 ng mL⁻¹ (covering approximately
5 orders of magnitude with 10,000-fold serum dilution), comprehensively encompassing both
infection monitoring and cardiovascular risk assessment ranges
• Calibration: The quantitative conversion is achieved through a linear calibration model (R² =
0.999) as shown in Fig. 4f
We are particularly grateful for this suggestion, as the additional validation has significantly
strengthened our study by unequivocally demonstrating that the DBDIY platform serves not as
merely a qualitative tool, but as a highly sensitive and precise quantitative platform with
performance directly benchmarked against clinical gold standards. This robust validation confirms
its potential for demanding clinical applications including cardiovascular risk stratification and
sepsis monitoring.

replication. To address the concern about statistical power, we have significantly increased the
sample size for the experiment presented in Fig. 2. The study now includes 12 mice per group
(control and LPS-injected), up from the initial 4, and this is clearly stated in the revised figure legend.
Regarding technical replicates, each biological sample (serum or whole blood from a single mouse)
was assayed once on the array. However, within that single assay, the signal for each analyte was
measured from four replicate spots. To ensure robustness, the spot with the highest deviation was
excluded, and the mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) was calculated from the remaining three
spots, as described in the Methods. This approach provides a reliable technical measurement for
each biological replicate while conserving precious sample volume. The increased sample size
(n=12 biologically independent samples per group) now provides substantial power for the
statistical comparisons made.

To further strengthen the clinical validation of our platform, we conducted an additional

Response: We thank the reviewer for raising these important methodological considerations
regarding the comparison with CBA. We acknowledge the observed quantitative differences
between the platforms, where the absolute concentrations measured by our DBDIY array were
generally lower than those obtained by CBA (Fig. R2). This discrepancy can be reasonably attributed
to several methodological factors.
First, there are inherent standardization differences between the platforms, as each employs
distinct antibody pairs and reference standards calibrated through independent systems.
Second, the fundamental detection principles differ substantially. CBA utilizes bead-based
fluorescence detection in solution, whereas our DBDIY platform relies on surface-based capture
combined with plasmon-enhanced fluorescence, which may affect binding kinetics and signal
generation. Finally, matrix interactions and solid-phase binding efficiency may vary between the
two systems, potentially influencing absolute recovery rates.
Despite these expected technical variations in absolute quantification, it is important to emphasize
that both platforms demonstrated excellent concordance in detecting the same biological trends.
All seven cytokines showed statistically significant and consistent elevation patterns in response to
anti-CD3/28 stimulation across both methods.
While a formal matrix effects study was beyond the scope of this initial technology validation, the
consistent response patterns observed across multiple cytokines in complex cell culture
supernatants provide indirect evidence that matrix effects are comparably managed in both
systems.
The consistent biological conclusions drawn from both platforms, despite technical differences in
absolute quantification, strongly support the validity and utility of our DBDIY array for functional
immune monitoring applications where relative changes and response patterns are of primary
importance.

Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this practical consideration regarding the
manual spotting process. We acknowledge that achieving perfect alignment by freehand pipetting
alone can be challenging, which is why we have systematically evaluated both the operational ease
and technical robustness of our approach.
In direct response to this concern, we have provided three supplementary videos that visually
demonstrate the operational workflow. Supplementary Video 1 illustrates the complete DBDIY
process, showing how a standard pipette interacts with our patterned chip. Supplementary Video
2 specifically highlights the system's built-in tolerance to pipetting position deviations, confirming
that the hydrophilic-hydrophobic interface effectively self-guides and confines droplets even with
intentional misalignment. Most notably, Supplementary Video 3 demonstrates continuous manual
spotting of over 100 spots in a routine and efficient manner, providing direct evidence of the
method's practicality.
These visual demonstrations are supported by quantitative data in Supplementary Fig. 1, where
we deliberately introduced positional deviations and found no significant impact on final
fluorescence signals. This confirms that the chip's patterned design provides intrinsic spatial
guidance, making the process robust to normal variations in manual pipetting.
While we demonstrate that optional, low-cost guides can further enhance consistency for high-
throughput applications, the core technology requires only a standard pipette to achieve reliable
results. This stands in clear contrast to systems requiring expensive, high-precision robotic
plotters. We have revised the manuscript to more precisely describe the operational requirements as
"a pipette, aided by the intrinsic guiding properties of the patterned chip."

It would be useful to comment on drying of the devices for storage and testing. The use of water

without protective layers?
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding protein stability during drying, which is indeed a critical consideration for any solid-phase immunoassay. In response to the question of whether drying such surfaces without protective layers is normal practice, we would like to clarify that the process of drying spotted capture antibodies to immobilize them on a solid surface is in fact a well established and widely used method in the fabrication of both commercial and research based protein microarrays (Ref. 17-29).
In our current protocol, the capture antibodies were prepared in a standard phosphate buffered
saline (PBS) solution. The chemical composition of the spotting buffer, including ionic strength and
pH, plays a key role in helping maintain protein structural integrity during the brief drying and
immobilization process. This conventional approach has proven effective for laboratory based
immunoassays, as supported by the high sensitivity and specificity achieved in our study. These
performance metrics confirm that under our controlled conditions, the drying process did not
compromise the assay's functionality.
Looking ahead, we completely agree that developing a formulation for robust, long-term storage
is a vital next step. This would vitrify upon drying, creating a protective microenvironment around
the immobilized antibodies and enabling the development of a ready-to-use, shelf-stable product.

Reviewer #3:
Thank you for the authors’ efforts in revising the manuscript. The additional data and clarifications
have improved several aspects of the work and in general, the paper is an example of good
scientific work. However, some important points related to the clinical relevance, interpretation of
diagnostic performance, and methodological transparency remain insufficiently addressed.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the constructive feedback and for acknowledging the
improvements made. We agree that clinical relevance, diagnostic performance interpretation, and
methodological transparency are essential for evaluating any novel diagnostic platform. Below we
address these points in detail.
• Clinical relevance and diagnostic performance interpretation
We recognize that direct comparison of absolute concentration values between different
immunoassay platforms can be challenging due to inherent variations in reagents, detection
principles, calibration, and data processing. Therefore, in validating our DBDIY platform, we
focused on demonstrating its ability to accurately reflect clinically relevant biological trends rather
than pursuing perfect numerical agreement with a reference method that uses fundamentally
different reagents and detection principles.
This approach is well established in the validation of novel diagnostic technologies, as it prioritizes
correct identification of biomarker patterns, such as elevated CRP during infection or cytokine
dynamics upon immune stimulation, over absolute concentration concordance. Our results show
strong correlation (R² > 0.9) and acceptable limits of agreement in Bland-Altman analysis across a
large cohort of clinical samples, confirming that the DBDIY platform reliably captures the same
biological variations as the clinical reference method. This supports its suitability for clinical
screening and longitudinal monitoring in volume-limited settings.
• Enhancing methodological transparency
To further improve transparency, we have now clearly specified both concentration-based and raw-
signal-based cutoff values. We have also converted the fluorescence signals for CRP and NT-proBNP
into concentration units to facilitate visual assessment of diagnostic agreement. Statistically
inappropriate ROC curve depictions have been removed and replaced with confidence intervals
and Bland-Altman analyses. These revisions provide a clearer and more statistically rigorous
presentation of the platform’s diagnostic performance and enhance the reproducibility of our
assay protocol.
We believe these clarifications and additions have strengthened the clinical relevance and
methodological transparency of our study, and we thank the reviewer for prompting these
important improvements.
- Abstract: the concept of high-throughput measurement of protein levels in small-volume
biological fluids does not seem compatible with the expression “especially in children (neonates?),
specific disease patients, and experimental animals.” In the context of clinical diagnosis and
laboratory testing, it is not clear how experimental animals are relevant. This may be of greater
importance in the field of intensive care (ICU).
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful observation regarding the phrasing in the
Abstract. The original wording did indeed conflate two distinct application contexts, which could
lead to ambiguity. To clarify the scope and relevance of our platform, we have revised the sentence
to clearly separate its clinical diagnostic value (particularly for vulnerable populations including
children and critically ill patients) from its preclinical utility (enabling longitudinal monitoring in
experimental animals). This modification ensures that the distinct importance of small-volume,
high-throughput protein measurement in each setting is unambiguously communicated.

In the Revised Manuscript (Page 2), the following paragraph was refined:
“Accurate, high-throughput measurement of protein levels in small-volume biological fluids is
critical in both clinical and laboratory settings1-3. For clinical diagnosis and prognosis, this is
especially vital in vulnerable populations such as children and critically ill patients. In preclinical

- The cutoffs formulated on the basis of the raw signal between the clinical methods and the DBDIY
assay differ (Figure 4b, dashed lines).
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising the point regarding the different cutoff lines in Fig. 4b.
The visual distinction arises because the two lines are plotted using different units. The DBDIY
cutoff is drawn based on the corresponding raw fluorescence signal, while the clinical cutoff is
reported as a concentration. This presentation choice was intentional, as we sought to avoid
potential bias introduced by inter-platform variations in standard sources, detection principles,
calibration models, and data processing, all of which can complicate direct concentration-based
comparisons.
To validate the quantitative performance of the DBDIY platform, we collected 112 pediatric
peripheral blood samples and measured CRP using both the DBDIY array and the clinical dry
fluorescence immunoassay (DFIA). To minimize the influence of differences in reference standards,
we constructed the calibration curve using samples with known clinical values. The derived
concentration results, as shown in Fig. 4, demonstrate that the DBDIY platform achieves 100%
sensitivity and specificity (95% CI: 95.2 to 100%) and a high correlation (R² = 0.940) with the clinical
method, whether based on raw fluorescence signals or on concentration values.
The strong concordance between the raw DBDIY signal and the clinical concentration indicates that
the platform can support semi-quantitative analysis and longitudinal monitoring without requiring
a standard curve (Supplementary Fig. 6). This feature is particularly valuable in resource-limited
settings, where results can be interpreted visually from the fluorescence pattern for relative trend
assessment. In laboratory or clinical settings requiring precise quantification, concentration values
can be obtained reliably via the standard calibration curve and data processing.
In summary, the use of raw signal for cutoff visualization reflects our methodological approach to
cross-platform comparison, while the additional validation with 112 samples confirms the
platform’s robust quantitative performance and operational flexibility.

- Sentence 243, “A cohort of 100 peripheral blood samples from children (50 positive and 50
negative)”, indicates that the samples were preselected according to the routine clinical cutoff.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this observation. We would like to clarify that the 100
pediatric peripheral blood samples were collected prospectively from children with suspected
infection, without any preselection based on prior CRP results. The study was conducted in a
blinded manner: the DBDIY operator was unaware of the clinical status or reference results, and
the clinical laboratory was unaware of the DBDIY results. After unblinding and analysis, we found
that 50 samples were classified as positive and 50 as negative by the clinical reference method.
To avoid any unintended implication of preselection, we have revised the text in the manuscript to
clearly state the blinded prospective collection process first, and to present the final count of 50
positive and 50 negative samples as an analytical outcome, not a selection criterion.
Revisions:
In the Revised Manuscript (Page 6), the following paragraph was refined:
"We then validated its quantitative detection capability using 112 peripheral blood samples
prospectively collected from children with suspected infection across multiple clinical departments,
including pediatric respiratory, pediatric emergency, neonatology, pediatric ICU, pediatric clinic,
and pediatric gastroenterology (Supplementary Table 2). The study was conducted in a blinded
manner. To minimize bias introduced by differences in reference standards, we constructed a
calibration curve using samples with known clinical values, thereby deriving concentration results
traceable to the clinical context. Following unblinding, 75 samples were classified as CRP-positive
and 37 as CRP-negative by the clinical dry fluorescence immunoassay (DFIA). Compared against
this clinical classification, the DBDIY array showed no false positives or false negatives, achieving
100% sensitivity and specificity (95% CI: 95.2% to 100%) (Fig. 4d)."
- For the newly developed method, the authors selected the cutoff at the maximum value of
Youden’s index, although this cutoff is not explicitly stated.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s attention to the cutoff selection process. All tests were
performed in a blinded manner. We conducted ROC analysis based on the positive/negative
classifications from the clinical reference methods (DFIA and CLIA) and initially identified the raw
fluorescence signal that yielded 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity as the cutoff for the DBDIY
array.
Considering the limited sample size in our current cohort, and to ensure the robustness and
generalizability of the cutoff across different assay conditions and future larger studies, we adopted
the threshold corresponding to the maximum Youden’s index as the reported cutoff criterion in
the main text. This approach is widely used and provides a balanced, statistically optimized
criterion that is less susceptible to small-sample variability.
Revisions:
In the Revised Manuscript (Page 13), the following paragraph was refined:
“Blinding procedure and cutoff determination
To minimize bias, all analyses were conducted in a blinded manner. The researchers performing the
DBDIY array assays and data analysis were unaware of the sample status (positive or negative) and
the results from the clinical reference methods. Similarly, clinical laboratory technicians conducting
the standard DFIA, immunoturbidimetry, and CLIA were unaware of the results generated by the
DBDIY platform. All experimental data were collected independently, and blinding was maintained
until all assays and initial data processing were completed. Afterward, results were unblinded for
final comparative analysis. Samples were excluded from the final comparative analysis if they had
insufficient volume for both analytical methods or if they showed gross hemolysis.
The diagnostic cutoff for the DBDIY array was determined based on the clinical classifications
(positive or negative) established by the reference methods. Under the blinded protocol, ROC
analysis was performed to identify the raw fluorescence signal corresponding to optimal
classification performance. In the present cohort, the threshold that yielded 100% sensitivity and
100% specificity coincided with the point of maximum Youden’s index. To ensure statistical
robustness and generalizability across assay conditions and future studies, we adopted this
threshold, corresponding to the maximum Youden’s index, as the reported cutoff. This widely
accepted approach provides a balanced and resilient criterion for diagnostic threshold selection,
regardless of sample size.”
- It is unusual that both cutoffs in Figures 4b and 9b are defined using raw signals, as cutoffs are
typically applied to analyte concentrations. It would be valuable to see how the agreement
between both cutoffs (new and established) appears when expressed in final concentration units,
and to compare these with those used in routine clinical practice. It would also be helpful to add
cutoffs and/or error grids to Figure 4g to visualize not only analytical but also clinical agreement.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding cutoff presentation.
We acknowledge that diagnostic cutoffs are conventionally expressed in concentration units, and
we appreciate the opportunity to clarify our methodology and the steps we have taken to enhance
interpretability.
In our initial analysis, we presented cutoffs based on raw fluorescence signals to facilitate a direct
calibration-independent comparison of signal distribution between positive and negative samples.
This approach highlights the inherent separation capability of our raw data and is particularly
relevant for demonstrating the platform's potential for semi-quantitative visual assessment.
However, we fully agree with the reviewer that alignment with established clinical practice requires
evaluation in concentration terms. To address this, we have now performed the following
additional analyses and modifications to the manuscript:
We have derived concentration values for all clinical samples using our calibration curves. In the
revised Manuscript (Fig. 4d for CRP and Extended Data Fig. 9 for NT-proBNP), we present direct
comparisons between DBDIY-derived concentrations and the reference method concentrations.
These plots include the established clinical decision thresholds, allowing for a clear visual
assessment of diagnostic agreement in standard units.
These revisions provide the requested concentration-based comparison and integrate visual cues
for clinical concordance directly into the main analytical figures. We believe these additions
significantly strengthen the clinical interpretability of our validation data and align the presentation
more closely with standard diagnostic reporting.
We are grateful for this insightful suggestion, which has improved the clarity and clinical relevance
of our data presentation.

- For the Bland–Altman analysis (new figure 4h), the limits of agreement were calculated and could
be discussed. For the serum assay measured from the same sample, limits of ±75% are very high.
Response: We acknowledge the reviewer’s observation regarding the width of the limits of
agreement (LoA ±75%) in the Bland-Altman analysis. This degree of variability is not uncommon
when comparing immunoassays based on fundamentally different principles, specifically our solid-
phase, plasmonic enhanced fluorescence platform versus the solution-phase immunoturbidimetry
reference method, which employs distinct antibody pairs, calibrators, and signal generation
mechanisms.
A closer inspection of the data points contributing to the wider LoA, as exemplified by the samples
listed in Table R1 (e.g., #5, #46, #85, #119, #138), reveals that a substantial proportion of the
observed dispersion occurs in the low concentration region. In these cases, the DBDIY platform
frequently reported higher values than immunoturbidimetry, suggesting a difference in analytical
sensitivity between the two methods. This pattern is consistent with the enhanced low-end
detection capability often afforded by plasmonic enhanced substrates, indicating that our method
may retain better performance near the lower limit of quantification.
Importantly, despite these quantifiable differences in absolute values, which are expected between
such distinct platforms, the mean bias was minimal (-0.96%) and the correlation was exceptionally
high (R² = 0.973). This confirms that both methods capture the same clinical trends and biological
variations, which is the primary criterion for a screening and monitoring tool. The calculated LoA
provides a transparent and useful measure of the expected inter-method variability for result
interpretation in practice.

- The authors state that “Collectively, the DBDIY array demonstrated excellent performance in
quantitatively detecting CRP levels in whole blood and serum samples, enabling faster and more
accurate diagnosis of infections in children, as well as effective monitoring of infection progression
trends (Extended Data Fig. 8).” However, the data in Figure 8 suggest that the DBDIY platform can
deliver results within 10 minutes to 1 hour, which is comparable to the normal clinical turnaround
time for CRP (approximately 10 minutes). The data presented in Figure 8 do not allow any
conclusions regarding result accuracy.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this critical and constructive observation. We fully agree
that the original statement overinterpreted the data presented in Extended Data Fig. 8, which
demonstrates the platform’s protocol flexibility and signal stability under shortened incubation
conditions and does not indicate a direct comparative advantage in diagnostic speed or accuracy
over established clinical CRP tests.
To address this, we have revised the relevant text in the manuscript to accurately reflect the
intended message:
The claim of enabling “faster and more accurate diagnosis” has been removed.
The role of Extended Data Fig. 8 is now clearly described as illustrating how the high sensitivity of
the platform allows for a reduction in sample dilution, thereby shortening the total assay time
while maintaining classification agreement with the clinical reference.

Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. In response, we have removed the
original ROC curve (Figure 9d) and performed an additional validation study using 30 independent
clinical serum samples. NT-proBNP was measured on these samples with both the DBDIY platform
and the clinical chemiluminescence immunoassay (CLIA). The fluorescence signals obtained from
the DBDIY array were converted to concentration values using a standard calibration curve. As
shown in Supplementary Fig. 8, excellent agreement was observed between the two methods,
whether comparing raw fluorescence signals or derived concentrations. The correlation analysis
for the concentration values yielded a high coefficient (R² > 0.95), confirming the quantitative
reliability of the DBDIY platform for NT-proBNP detection.
